content: In mathematics, a step function, also known as a staircase function, is defined as a function on the real numbers that can be expressed as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals. Informally, a step function is a piecewise constant function with only a finite number of pieces. Definition and First Consequences A function ( f: mathbb{R} to mathbb{R} ) is called a step function if it can be written in the form: [ f(x) = sum_{i=1}^n alpha_i chi_{A_i}(x) ] where ( n geq 0 ), ( alpha_i ) are real numbers, ( A_i ) are intervals, and ( chi_{A_i} ) is the indicator function of the interval ( A_i ). The indicator function ( chi_{A_i}(x) ) equals 1 if ( x in A_i ) and 0 otherwise. In this definition, the intervals ( A_i ) can be assumed to satisfy the following two properties: 1. The intervals are disjoint, meaning ( A_i cap A_j = emptyset ) for ( i neq j ). 2. The union of all intervals ( A_i ) covers the entire real line, i.e., ( bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i = mathbb{R} ). If these properties are not initially satisfied, a different set of intervals can be chosen to ensure they hold. Examples 1. A constant function is a trivial example of a step function. In this case, there is only one interval, ( A_0 = mathbb{R} ), and the function takes the same value everywhere. 2. The Heaviside function ( H(x) ) is a significant example of a step function. It is widely used in mathematics and engineering as the basis for test signals, such as those used to determine the step response of dynamical systems. 3. The rectangular function, also known as the normalized boxcar function, is another simple step function. It is often used to model a unit pulse. Non-Examples The integer part function (also known as the floor function) is not a step function under this definition because it has an infinite number of steps. Properties 1. The sum and product of two step functions are also step functions. Similarly, multiplying a step function by a real number results in another step function. Consequently, step functions form an algebra over the real numbers. 2. A step function takes only a finite number of distinct values. If the intervals ( A_i ) in the definition are disjoint and their union is the entire real line, then ( f(x) = alpha_i ) for all ( x in A_i ). 3. The integral of a step function over the real line can be computed as: [ int f(x) , dx = sum_{i=1}^n alpha_i ell(A_i) ] where ( ell(A_i) ) represents the length of the interval ( A_i ). It is assumed here that all intervals ( A_i ) have finite length. This equality can serve as the starting point for constructing the Lebesgue integral.
